passages.t: The LORD appears a second time
passages.happening:
When Solomon has finished the house of the LORD and the palace, ‘and had achieved all that he had desired to do’ (verse 1), the LORD appears to him a second time, as he had at Gibeon (verse 2). “I have heard your prayer and petition before Me” (verse 3). God has set the temple apart by putting his Name there forever, and his eyes and his heart will be there for all time.

Then come two roads. If Solomon walks before God as David did, ‘with a heart of integrity and uprightness’ (verse 4), God will establish his throne over Israel forever, as he promised David (verse 5). ‘But if indeed you or your sons turn away from following Me’ (verse 6), and go to serve other gods, God will cut Israel off from the land and cast the temple from his presence, and Israel will become ‘an object of scorn and ridicule among all peoples’ (verse 7). The temple will become ‘a heap of rubble’ (verse 8). Those who pass by will ask why the LORD has done this, and the answer will be that the people forsook the LORD who brought them out of Egypt, and embraced other gods (verses 8-9).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 8 ended at the high point of Israel's story so far. Chapter 9 answers Solomon's prayer, and the answer has two edges. God accepts the temple and puts his Name there, but everything now depends on faithfulness.

The speech is built as a pair of conditions, a road of faithfulness and a road of turning away, much like the promises and warnings at the end of Deuteronomy. It even imagines a conversation among passers-by, who ask why the land lies ruined and are told the answer. Deuteronomy uses the same device.

The word integrity, in Hebrew tom, does not mean sinlessness; David's failures were well known. It means wholeness of loyalty, a heart undivided in its devotion to the LORD. Chapter 11 will say that Solomon's heart was not whole in exactly this sense.

God's promise to David stands, and each king's share in it depends on obedience. The chapter holds together God's unbreakable commitment and the real results of unfaithfulness, a tension the rest of Kings works out. The warning hangs over 1 and 2 Kings, which end with what it describes: a people cut off from the land, and the temple a heap of rubble.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy pictures the same scene: the nations will ask why the LORD has done this to the land, and the people will answer, ‘It is because they abandoned the covenant of the LORD, the God of their fathers’ (Deuteronomy 29:25).

Jeremiah stood in the temple court and warned those who trusted in the building: “therefore what I did to Shiloh I will now do to the house that bears My Name, the house in which you trust” (Jeremiah 7:14).
passages.asks: God's word to Solomon at the height of his success was a warning. Ask what you most need to hear from God when things are going well. And ask whether your heart is whole toward him, or only mostly.

passages.happening: At the end of the twenty years in which Solomon built the two houses, the house of the LORD and the palace (verse 10), he gives Hiram king of Tyre twenty towns in the land of Galilee, for Hiram had supplied cedar, cypress and gold for everything he wanted (verse 11). Hiram comes to see them and is not pleased. “What are these towns you have given me, my brother?” (verse 13), he asks, and he calls them the Land of Cabul. “And Hiram had sent the king 120 talents of gold” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Kings in that world sealed treaties with gifts, marriages and land. The twenty towns in Galilee were payment for Hiram's timber and gold, or a pledge against it. Hiram addresses Solomon as his brother, the language treaty partners used of each other.

The meaning of Cabul is uncertain. Many readers hear a Hebrew pun suggesting something like as good as nothing. A talent was a large weight of metal, roughly thirty kilograms, so a hundred and twenty talents of gold was an enormous sum.

The note fits a pattern in this chapter. A list of deals and works follows straight after God's warning, as if to let the reader weigh each achievement against the conditions just laid down. The word desire comes back again and again (verses 1, 11, 19), a quiet note that Solomon built whatever he wanted.
passages.later: Chronicles tells it the other way: ‘Solomon rebuilt the cities Hiram had given him and settled Israelites there’ (2 Chronicles 8:2). Some readers think that Hiram, displeased, gave the towns back and Solomon then rebuilt them; others that the towns changed hands within a larger deal, and that each book tells a different side of it.
passages.asks: Hiram was not pleased with what he was given. Ask whether you have kept your side of an agreement in a way you would be glad to have inspected. And ask whether you give your best or your leftovers to those who have served you.

passages.t: Forced labor, and the cities Solomon built
passages.happening:
“This is the account of the forced labor that King Solomon imposed” (verse 15) to build the house of the LORD, his palace, the terraces, the wall of Jerusalem, and Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer. Pharaoh had captured Gezer, burned it, killed its Canaanite people and given it to his daughter as a dowry. Solomon rebuilt it, with Lower Beth-horon, Baalath and Tamar in the wilderness, and his store cities and his cities for chariots and horses, ‘whatever he desired to build’ (verses 16-19).

The peoples who remained in the land, Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, Solomon conscripted ‘to be forced laborers, as they are to this day’ (verse 21). ‘But Solomon did not consign any of the Israelites to slavery’ (verse 22). They were his soldiers, officials and commanders, and five hundred and fifty of them supervised the work (verses 22-23).

When Pharaoh's daughter moves from the City of David into the palace built for her, Solomon builds the terraces (verse 24). Three times a year he offers burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar he built for the LORD (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer guarded the main roads through the land. In the twentieth century Yigael Yadin found similar six-chambered gates at all three and credited them to Solomon because of this verse. Other archaeologists, especially those who hold a lower dating for this period, such as Israel Finkelstein, date those gates to the following century. The debate is live, and it is about how large Solomon's kingdom was more than whether it existed.

The pharaoh who took Gezer belonged to Egypt's Twenty-first Dynasty; Siamun is often suggested, but the text does not name him. The written Hebrew of verse 18 reads Tamar, a town in the southern wilderness, while the traditional reading and Chronicles have Tadmor, the oasis later called Palmyra; the BSB follows the written text.

Forced labor was a normal tool of ancient kings for building. Verses 20-22 set the remaining Canaanite peoples, conscripted for good, apart from the Israelites, who served as soldiers, officers and supervisors.

The three yearly sacrifices match the three pilgrim feasts of the law, Unleavened Bread, Weeks and Tabernacles, when every Israelite man was to appear before the LORD.
passages.later: The law set the three feasts: ‘Three times a year all your men are to appear before the LORD your God in the place He will choose’ (Deuteronomy 16:16). And the book of Judges records the forced labor of the Canaanites long before Solomon: ‘When Israel became stronger, they pressed the Canaanites into forced labor, but they never drove them out completely’ (Judges 1:28).
passages.hard:
Verse 22 says that Solomon made no Israelites slaves, but 5:13 and 12:4 describe Israelites laboring under a heavy yoke. Which is it?

Most interpreters see two systems. The permanent forced labor of verses 20-21 fell on the remaining Canaanite peoples, while Israelites served in a rotating levy, one month in three according to 5:13-14, and in military and supervisory posts. The text does not pretend the levy was light. The northern tribes' complaint in chapter 12 shows that it was felt as a yoke, and the narrator lets the complaint stand. Some scholars think verse 22 reflects an idealizing source; others think it simply marks a difference of status, slave and conscript.

Either way, the book does not hold up Solomon's labor policy as a model. It records the conscription of the Canaanite peoples as a fact of the period, not as something God commanded. Earlier books count such forced labor as a failure to keep God's command, and it is troubling in itself.

A word for anyone who is being held, owned or forced to work today. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The narrator lists the cities, and then the people who built them. Ask whose labor stands behind the things you are proud of. And ask whether you would call it fair if the labor were yours.

passages.happening: King Solomon also builds a fleet at Ezion-geber, near Eloth in Edom, on the shore of the Red Sea (verse 26). Hiram sends men who know the sea to serve with Solomon's men (verse 27). ‘They sailed to Ophir and imported gold from there’ (verse 28), four hundred and twenty talents, and brought it to Solomon.
passages.hearers:
Ezion-geber lay at the northern tip of the Gulf of Aqaba, one of the waters the Bible calls the Red Sea. A port there opened the trade of Arabia and beyond, and Hiram's sailors brought the skill of the sea.

Where Ophir lay is unknown. Southern Arabia, East Africa and India have all been proposed. Its name became a byword for fine gold.

The chapter that opened with God's warning closes with gold arriving by ship. The next chapter shows how much.
passages.later: A royal psalm pictures a queen ‘adorned with the gold of Ophir’ (Psalm 45:9). And Job, speaking of wisdom, sets the gold of Ophir beside it and finds the gold wanting: “It cannot be valued in the gold of Ophir, in precious onyx or sapphire” (Job 28:16).
passages.asks: Gold came by sea through a partnership with a foreign king. Ask what riches you are reaching for, and why. And ask what the warning at the start of this chapter would say to the wealth at its end.
